title: Are these two lines really bent?
description: Two upright lines run through a burst of spokes and seem to bend outwards. A ruler shows each line is straight, and equal gaps show the lines are parallel. Keeko trusts the eye and says the lines are bent.
teaching_notes: One idea: a ruler and a measured gap can overrule what the eye seems to see. Watch for students who trust the picture and say the lines are bent.

source: In a picture, two upright lines run through a burst of spoke
video_script.why: The child checks that a line is straight with a ruler, checks that two lines are parallel by measuring equal gaps, and sees that crossing lines can trick the eye.
video_script.substitution: the book's own picture: two upright lines running through a burst of spokes, seeming to bend outwards in the middle
video_script.anchor: two upright lines running through a burst of spokes, seeming to bend outwards in the middle
video_script.wrong_move: trusts what the eye seems to see and does not check with a ruler or a measured gap
video_script.payoff_line: A measurement can overrule what the eye seems to see

final_answer.value: The lines are straight and parallel; the crossing spokes trick the eye about angles
final_answer.spoken: the lines are straight and parallel, and the crossing spokes trick the eye about angles

hold_back: The lines are straight and parallel; the crossing spokes trick the eye about angles
maths_rules: a straight line fits the edge of a ruler all along its length
parallel lines keep the same gap everywhere
measure the gap at the top, the middle and the bottom; equal gaps show the lines are parallel
the spokes cut the lines at many different angles, and the eye misjudges the angles, so the lines seem to bend
video_script.design: One picture for the whole video. The ruler slides along each line, and the gap is shown by a double arrow at three heights.
